blocks.p: Five files do the work, and you meet them in order. Customer.cs holds one customer. CustomerData.cs calls the five customer stored procedures from chapter 4. Grid.cs tidies any grid. frmCustomers.cs is the list. frmCustomerEdit.cs is the add and edit form. At the end, two small classes for the services and the suppliers follow the same pattern, and you write the Supplier pair yourself.

words: Class
A description of one kind of thing, written as code. The Customer class describes what one customer has: a number, two names, a phone, an email and a date.
Object
One real thing made from a class. The class is the plan; the object is one customer, with real names in it.
Property
One piece of information inside a class, such as FirstName. The program can read a property and, usually, change it.
Method
A named piece of code that does one job, such as Search or Tidy. Writing the name with brackets after it runs the job.
Constructor
The method that runs when an object is made with the word new. A form's constructor can take a value, and this chapter's edit form takes the customer's number.
Static
A class marked static has no objects made from it. You call its methods by the class name, such as CustomerData.Search, the way you called Db in chapter 5.
Grid
The DataGridView control: a table on a form, with a heading row and one row per record. In the code it is called dgvCustomers.
DataTable
A table of rows held in memory after the database answered. Db.GetTable gives one back, and a grid can show it.
Event
Something that happens to a control: a click, a key typed, a row picked. An event method is the code that runs when that happens.
null
The value that means nothing is there at all. An empty email box becomes null, so the database stores NULL and not an empty piece of text.
bool
A value that is either true or false. The form uses one called picked to switch two buttons on or off.
DialogResult
The answer a small window gives when it closes: OK or Cancel. The list form waits for it, and loads the grid again on OK.

screens.title: A class holds one customer in the program.

blocks.p: In chapter 4, a customer was one row of the Customer table: a number, two names, a phone, an email and a date. Inside the program a customer needs a shape too, so that the form can hand one whole customer to the data class in a single go, instead of five separate values that could be passed in the wrong order. That shape is a class.

A class is a description of one kind of thing. It lists the pieces of information the thing has, and each piece is called a property. One real customer made from the class is called an object. The class below has one property for each column of the Customer table, and one extra property, FullName, which works out its own answer from the two names.

screens.title: Read how CustomerData talks to the five customer stored procedures.

blocks.p: A data class is the only place in the program that names a stored procedure. CustomerData has one method for each customer stored procedure from chapter 4, and every method is the same shape: give Db the procedure's name and its parameters, and hand back what comes out. The class is static, so you never make a CustomerData object: you write CustomerData.Search, the way you wrote Db.GetTable in chapter 5.

Read it region by region. A region is a fold in the editor, marked #region and #endregion, that groups the lines for one job. Search and Delete are two lines each. GetByID turns one row into one Customer object. Add is the interesting one: the stored procedure hands back the new customer's number through an output parameter, and Db.Out makes that parameter.

code.title: Data/CustomerData.cs: one method for each stored procedure
parts: System.Data gives DataTable and DataRow. System.Data.SqlClient gives SqlParameter, the type Db.P and Db.Out make. using BikeShop.Models lets the file say Customer. The class is static: no objects, only methods called by the class name.
Search: the rows whose name or phone contains the text

Search hands Db.GetTable the name of the stored procedure and one parameter, made by Db.P. Whatever usp_Customer_Search selects comes back as a DataTable, and the form gives that table to the grid. An empty search text matches every customer.
GetByID: one customer as an object

The stored procedure answers with a table of one row, or no rows. No rows means there is no such customer, and the method returns null: nothing at all. Otherwise row is that one row, and each column is copied into a new Customer object. (int) and (string) in front of a column say what kind of value is inside. Email can be NULL in the database, which arrives as DBNull.Value, so the method checks for that first and stores null in the object.
Add: save a new customer, and get the new number back

usp_Customer_Add has two output parameters: @NewCustomerID and @Message. Db.Run makes @Message itself, so this method makes the other one with Db.Out, and keeps hold of it in newID. Db.Run returns the message: an empty string when the save worked, or a sentence to show the user. When the message is empty, the number the database chose is read from newID.Value and put into the customer object, so the caller knows it.
Update: save changes to a customer who already has a number
Five parameters go in, one for each box on the edit form plus the number that says which row to change. Nothing comes back except the message.
Delete: ask the database to take one customer out

Only the number goes in. The stored procedure from chapter 4 refuses when the customer has bookings or sales, and its sentence comes back as the message. The last two braces end the class and the namespace.

screens.title: What a grid shows, and why it needs tidying.

blocks.p: A grid is the DataGridView control: a table on a form with a heading row and one row per record. Give a grid a DataTable and it shows every column, with the column's name as the heading. Left alone, that means a heading like CustomerID, which is a number the user never needs, and a heading like DateJoined, which runs two words together.

Grid.cs is a small helper, written once and used by every grid in the program. Its method Tidy hides the columns you name, turns every heading into plain words, shows money with a pound sign and two decimal places, and shows dates as a day name and a date. The rule for the user is simple to state: names, never numbers. Two more methods, SelectedID and SelectedText, read one value from the row the user has picked.

Grid.cs goes at the top of the project, beside Program.cs, Session.cs and Msg.cs, because every form uses it. In Visual Studio 2019 that means adding the class to the project line itself, not to a folder.

screens.title: Read the Grid helper.

code.title: Grid.cs: the helpers every grid uses
parts: System.Text gives StringBuilder, which the Words method uses to build a heading one letter at a time. System.Windows.Forms gives DataGridView. The class is static and sits in the BikeShop namespace itself, so every form can say Grid without a using line.
Tidy: the grid, and the columns to hide

Tidy takes the grid and then any number of column names, which params gathers into a list called hiddenColumns. A form writes Grid.Tidy(dgvCustomers, "CustomerID") with one name, and a form with two number columns writes two.

foreach looks at each name in the list in turn. If the grid has a column with that name, its Visible setting is switched to false. The column is still there, so SelectedID can read the hidden number later.
This foreach looks at every column of the grid. HeaderText is the words the user sees at the top of the column, and Words turns the column's name into them: DateJoined becomes Date joined.

ValueType is the kind of value the column holds. decimal is the kind for money. When the column holds decimals and its name says money, IsMoney answers true, and the column is shown with a pound sign and two decimal places, pushed to the right the way money is written.

A DateTime column is shown as a day name, a day, a month and a year, such as Mon 12 Oct 2026. If the column's name contains the word Time, the hours and minutes are shown instead, because the diary grids in chapter 7 show one day at a time. The closing braces end the if, the else if and the foreach.
A grid picks its first row by itself as soon as it is filled. ClearSelection undoes that, so the form starts with no row picked and Edit and Delete switched off.
IsMoney answers true when the column's name contains any of the seven money words. The two vertical bars mean or: any one match is enough. private means only Grid itself can call this method.

Words walks along the column's name one letter at a time. char is one letter. When a capital letter follows a small one, a space goes in and the capital becomes small. StringBuilder collects the letters, and ToString hands back the finished heading.
SelectedID: the hidden number of the picked row

SelectedRows is the list of rows the user has picked. When the list is empty the method returns 0, which every form treats as nothing picked. Otherwise it reads the named cell of the first picked row and turns the value into a whole number.
SelectedText: a text value from the picked row
The same shape, for text: an empty string when nothing is picked, otherwise the named cell as text. The delete button uses this to put the customer's name into its question.
